title: Dog allergies: the signs, the types, and what actually helps
dek: Constant licking, scratching and ear infections usually aren't random. Here's how to tell if it's allergies, what kind, and what to do about it.
description: Itchy paws, ear infections, red skin? How to tell if your dog has allergies, the four main types, which tests work, and what actually helps.

glance.label: The #1 sign of allergies in dogs
How long a food allergy trial takes

body.title: When it's an emergency
body.text: If your dog's face suddenly swells, they break out in hives, or they're vomiting, drooling, weak or struggling to breathe after a sting, a new food or a medicine, go to the nearest emergency vet now. That can be a severe allergic reaction, and it needs treatment right away.

children.text: When people think of allergies, they think of sneezing and watery eyes. Dogs mostly don't do that. Dogs itch. They lick their paws, scratch their ears, rub their face on the carpet and chew at their belly, and a lot of owners don't connect it to allergies until it's been going on for months.
You're not alone if that's your dog. At Nationwide pet insurance, skin allergies have been
the #1 reason for dog claims

13 years in a row. Allergies can't be cured, but they can be managed well. The sooner you figure out what's going on, the less your dog suffers, and the less you spend chasing the same infection over and over.
The signs: it's mostly itch
Allergies in dogs show up in the skin and ears first. Here's what to watch for:
Licking or chewing the paws,
sometimes until the fur between the toes turns reddish-brown from saliva.
Rubbing the face
on the floor or furniture, or pawing at the eyes and muzzle.
Ear problems that keep coming back:
head shaking, scratching at the ears, a bad smell or brown gunk. In some dogs,
repeat ear infections are the only sign
Red skin, bumps or a rash,
especially on the belly, armpits and groin.
Hair loss, scabs or hot spots
from scratching, and over time, skin that turns darker or thicker.
A yeasty or musty smell,
which often means an infection has started on top of the allergy.
Vomiting, diarrhea, gas or extra poops,
mostly with food allergies.
Sneezing or watery eyes.
It happens, but far less than in people. Only
about 15% of dogs
with environmental allergies get nose or airway symptoms.
Where your dog itches can be a clue. Paws, face, ears and belly usually point to environmental or food allergies. Itching along the lower back, tail and back legs usually points to fleas.
The four main types of dog allergies

cells: Flea saliva. [One bite can itch for days](https://vcahospitals.com/know-your-pet/allergy-flea-allergy-dermatitis-in-dogs).
Itch and hair loss from the middle of the back to the tail and down the back legs. You may never see a flea.
Pollen, grass, weeds, mold, dust mites

Paws, face, ears, belly and armpits. Usually starts between [6 months and 3 years old](https://www.merckvetmanual.com/dog-owners/skin-disorders-of-dogs/allergies-in-dogs), and often seasonal at first.
Usually a protein. Beef, chicken, dairy, eggs, wheat and soy are common culprits.
The same itch, but it doesn't change with the seasons. Sometimes stomach trouble too. Can start at any age.
Something the skin touches: certain plants, mulch, carpet cleaners, fabrics
Only where fur is thin, like the belly, paws, chin and groin. [Fairly uncommon](https://www.petmd.com/dog/conditions/skin/contact-dermatitis).

children.text: Many dogs have more than one. A dog with environmental allergies can also be allergic to fleas, which is why one fix rarely solves everything.
Sudden reactions

Separate from the everyday itch, some dogs react within minutes to hours to a bee sting, a vaccine, a medicine or a food. The usual signs are hives and a puffy face or muzzle. That's uncomfortable but often not dangerous, so call your vet. Rarely, the reaction spreads through the body: vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, weakness, trouble breathing or pale or blue gums.
That's anaphylaxis
, and it's an emergency. Reactions can get worse each time, so tell your vet about any reaction, even a mild one.
Is it really allergies?

Allergies aren't the only thing that makes dogs itch. Mites (mange), ringworm and bacterial or yeast infections can look almost the same, and allergies often cause infections on top. That's why your vet will usually check for parasites and infection first, with quick tests like a skin scraping or a piece of tape pressed on the skin, before calling it allergies. As the
American Animal Hospital Association
puts it, "itching is a symptom, not a diagnosis."
How vets figure out which allergy it is
Rule out fleas first,
even if you've never seen one. Fleas only stay on a dog long enough to feed. The fix is steady flea prevention for every dog and cat in the house, all year.
Treat any infection.
Skin and ear infections make the itch worse and hide what's underneath.
Try a food trial if the itch is year-round.
Your dog eats only a prescription or specially chosen diet, with no treats, table scraps, flavored medicines or chews, for
up to 3 months
. If the itch clears, the old food goes back in. If the itch returns, usually within two weeks, you have your answer.
Test to plan treatment if it's environmental.
Skin or blood allergy tests can't tell you whether your dog has allergies, but they can show which pollens, molds or mites to target with allergy shots.

body.title: Skip the at-home allergy kits
body.text: Hair and saliva tests sold online, and blood tests for food allergies, aren't reliable. In one study, [water and fake fur tested "positive"](https://www.veterinarypracticenews.com/the-pros-and-cons-of-food-allergy-testing/) for food allergies. A food trial is still the only accurate way to diagnose a food allergy.

children.text: What actually helps
Allergies are managed, not cured. The goal isn't zero itching forever. It's a comfortable dog with fewer flare-ups. Most dogs do best with a mix of these:
Year-round flea prevention,
for every pet in the home. It's the simplest fix, and it helps even if fleas aren't the main problem.
Prescription itch relief.
Newer medicines work within a day or a few days:
daily pills like Apoquel and Zenrelia, and Cytopoint, a shot that lasts 4 to 8 weeks
. Steroids work fast too, but they have more side effects with long-term use.
Allergy shots or drops (immunotherapy)
for environmental allergies. It's the only treatment that changes how the immune system reacts, and
60% to 80% of dogs improve
. It's slow: it can take up to a year to know if it's working.
The right food
for food allergies: a prescription diet or one your vet helps you choose. Store-bought "limited ingredient" foods can contain traces of other proteins, which can ruin a food trial.
Skin care:
medicated or gentle shampoos, wiping paws and belly after walks in allergy season, and omega-3 supplements if your vet recommends them.
Treating infections early,
before a small hot spot or ear infection turns into a bigger, pricier problem.

body.title: Check before giving human allergy medicine
body.text: Some human allergy pills are used for dogs, but only at the dose your vet gives you. Many contain a decongestant like pseudoephedrine (often marked with a "D"), which can cause a racing heart, tremors and seizures in dogs. [Always ask your vet first](https://www.aspca.org/news/can-human-allergy-medication-be-harmful-pets-our-experts-explain), and see our guide to [what to do if your dog eats something it shouldn't](/blog/dog-ate-something-toxic-what-to-do).

children.text: What it might cost
Honest answer: allergies are often a long-term cost, not a one-time one. Most cases start with a regular exam, which we've broken down in
what a vet visit costs
. After that, it depends on the type: flea prevention is the cheapest, a food trial means a few months of special food, and ongoing itch medicine or allergy shots are a monthly expense.
Ask your vet for an estimate, and be upfront about your budget. There's usually more than one way to treat allergies, and a plan you can keep up with is better than a perfect one you can't.
When to see the vet
Itching, licking or chewing that lasts more than a couple of weeks
Ear infections that keep coming back
Open sores, hot spots, hair loss or a bad smell
Itching along with vomiting, diarrhea or weight loss
Right away, at an emergency vet: a swollen face with trouble breathing, vomiting or collapse
Common questions

items.q: Can dogs be allergic to grass?
items.a: Yes. Grass and weed pollens are some of the most common environmental allergens. These dogs often itch most in spring and summer, and you may notice them licking their paws or belly after walks. Wiping their paws and belly when you come inside can help.

items.q: Is grain-free food better for dogs with allergies?
items.a: Usually not. Most food allergies are to proteins like beef, chicken or dairy, not grains. Switching to grain-free doesn't test for a food allergy. A proper food trial with your vet does.

items.q: Can a dog suddenly develop allergies?
items.a: Yes. Environmental allergies usually start between 6 months and 3 years old, but a dog can become allergic to a food they've eaten for years. New itching in an adult dog is worth a vet visit.
Usually not. Allergies tend to be lifelong. The good news is that today's treatments make them much easier to manage than they were even a few years ago.

children.text: If your dog has been licking and scratching for a while, you're not imagining it, and you're not a bad owner for not catching it sooner. It's one of the most common things vets see, and one of the most treatable. Start with a vet visit, get the fleas and infections out of the way, and work from there.
